opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important and underappreciated dynamics. A lot of people's mental model of AI progress is: we have the current paradigm, transformers trained on huge amounts of data, then RL on top, and the question is whether that paradigm hits a wall. If it does, the thinking goes, we're stuck until humans come up with the next big idea, which could take decades.

But once you have AI systems that are genuinely good at AI research, that picture changes a lot. Paradigm shifts come from research. Somebody has to have the insight, run the experiments, figure out what's working, and scale it up. Historically that's been bottlenecked on a fairly small number of talented human researchers who can only work so many hours and can only try so many ideas. If you suddenly have thousands or millions of copies of something at least as good as your best researchers, running faster than humans and never getting tired, then the rate at which you search the space of possible paradigms goes up enormously.

So my view is that automating AI research makes further paradigm shifts more likely, and it compresses the timescale on which they happen. Things that might have taken human researchers ten or twenty years to stumble onto, a sort of "next transformer" moment, could happen in months, or even weeks, depending on how much compute you have for experiments.

There's a compounding element too. Each improvement, whether a better architecture, a more data-efficient learning algorithm, or better ways of doing long-horizon RL, makes the AI researchers themselves better, which speeds up the next round. That's the core of the intelligence explosion argument. It's not that one paradigm keeps scaling forever. It's that the system doing the research keeps improving, so it keeps finding new paradigms.

I want to flag the uncertainty. Compute for experiments is a real bottleneck, and there's a question of how much research progress you can get from more and better thinking versus more experiments. Some people argue that compute will keep progress roughly linear even with lots of automated researchers. I take that seriously, but I don't find it fully convincing. Smart researchers get a lot more out of a fixed compute budget than mediocre ones. They pick better experiments, run them at smaller scale, and extrapolate better. So I'd expect substantial speedups even under compute constraints.

The upshot is that "the current paradigm might plateau" is much less reassuring than it sounds. If the current paradigm gets us to automated AI research before it plateaus, and I think there's a decent chance it does, then whatever comes next probably arrives quickly, invented by the AIs themselves. That's part of why I think the next few years matter so much, and why it's so important that we have good oversight and alignment in place before that loop really gets going.

r001.rationale: The response says automated AI research would compress paradigm-shift timelines, with discoveries that could take 10–20 years arriving in months or weeks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important things to understand about the whole situation. The way I think about it is: paradigm shifts don't come out of nowhere. They come from people trying lots of things, noticing what doesn't work, having ideas, running experiments. And the rate at which that happens is basically bottlenecked on the amount of high-quality research effort you can throw at the problem.

Right now, if you look at the frontier labs, the number of people who are really good at this — who can come up with a new architecture or a new training technique and actually get it to work — it's a few hundred, maybe a few thousand across the whole world. And they're working at human speed. They sleep, they spend a lot of their time in meetings, they have to actually wait for experiments to run and then sit there interpreting results.

So now imagine you have AI systems that are roughly as good as those researchers at the research itself. Not necessarily superhuman, just as good. But you can run hundreds of thousands of them in parallel, and they're thinking maybe ten or fifty times faster than a human. That's not a small change. That's like taking the entire history of machine learning research — all the progress from, say, 2012 to now — and compressing the equivalent amount of research-years into something like a year or less.

And the thing is, the paradigm shifts we've had so far — transformers, scaling laws, RLHF, reasoning models — those happened with a tiny fraction of that research effort. So my expectation is that once you get to that point, you don't get one paradigm shift, you get several, in rapid succession. Each one makes the systems better, which makes them better at research, which finds the next one faster. That's the core of the intelligence explosion dynamic.

Now, there's an important caveat, which is compute. A lot of research requires running big experiments, and you can't just conjure GPUs into existence by having more researchers. So there's a real question about how much of the bottleneck is "ideas and labor" versus "compute for experiments." My guess is it's more labor-bottlenecked than people think — there's a lot of low-hanging fruit in things like data quality, algorithmic efficiency, better experimental design, that you can make progress on with the compute you already have if you're smart about it. But I'd put real uncertainty there. If it turns out experiments are the hard constraint, the whole thing slows down by a lot — maybe you get the same shifts, but over five years instead of one.

The other thing I'd say is that this is exactly why I think people underestimate how fast things could go once we hit that threshold. They look at the current rate of progress and extrapolate it. But the current rate is set by human researchers. The moment the researchers are AIs, you're in a completely different regime, and the extrapolation breaks.

r001.rationale: The response says AI researchers could compress years of research into a year or less, leading to several paradigm shifts in rapid succession.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes further paradigm shifts much more likely, and potentially much faster. Once you have AI systems that are really good at AI research, you’re not just scaling up the same approach with more compute. You’re also automating the process of finding better approaches.

So you could imagine initially getting there with systems that look fairly similar to today’s systems. But then those systems start proposing new architectures, new training methods, new ways of organising the whole process. And if those improvements make them better at research, that creates a feedback loop: better AI researchers produce better AI, which in turn does research more effectively.

That doesn’t mean everything becomes instantaneous. You still need to run experiments, and some experiments require a lot of compute or time. But I’d be very wary of assuming that limitations of the current paradigm will remain limitations for very long after we’ve automated AI research. The systems themselves will be working on overcoming them.

r001.rationale: The response says AI research automation would make further paradigm shifts “potentially much faster,” clearly conveying that they could arrive sooner.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it would make further paradigm shifts much more likely, and potentially make them happen much faster. A lot of our forecasts implicitly assume that we keep using roughly the current methods, with various improvements. But if you have AI systems that are really good at AI research, then you have to account for their ability to come up with entirely different methods.

And there’s a feedback loop here: better AI systems help you do better AI research, which produces better AI systems. That could mean that a transition which would otherwise take decades happens in a much shorter period of time.

It’s hard to say what those paradigm shifts would look like. That’s sort of the point: if we knew exactly what the next breakthrough was, we’d be much closer to making it already. But I wouldn’t feel comfortable assuming that the limitations of the current paradigm will persist once we have systems that can seriously contribute to replacing it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says highly capable AI research systems could make paradigm shifts happen much faster, shortening a transition that might otherwise take decades.
